title: Reading the public: programming dance music with a little jazz
summary: Briggs describes judging patrons' reactions in a cabaret, mixing a little jazz like Bugle Call Rag with melodic music, since Germans liked melody with a little beat.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, now this was, you were playing what, mostly dance music?

Yes, we had to arrange programs as I did. Even to the end of my career. We had to -- it was more or less a psychological judgment that I used, I could almost see by the expressions of certain clients, whether I should play for them.

After I noticed their reactions and everything else, and that was one of the main points an orchestra leader had to think of. You were playing for a certain type of people. If you're playing in a dance hall, there's no point. In a dance hall you're far
away from the public. But if you're playing in a cabaret where you're right next to them, you have to try and find out what they want, and give it to them.
Well, was there a lot of jazz mixed in there?

Yes, there was a little jazz, we played 'Bugle Call Rag.' We didn't play all jazz numbers, all night. We had another very, very fine number. It was called 'Up and At 'Em'. Those numbers you would choose when to play them. If you had some youngsters in the place, you'd know when you could use them, you see. But in general, the Germans loved authentic music, melody.
